topics.title: 21.1 Process abstraction
topics.summary: The process abstraction groups resources and identity. Its virtual address space determines which addresses have meaning; its descriptor table determines what small descriptor numbers refer to; its credentials help determine which requests are allowed. Two processes can use the integer descriptor 3 for entirely different files. A thread is an execution stream within that environment. Threads in one process usually share mappings and many resources while retaining their own register state and stacks. Therefore, “switching processes” and “switching threads” are related but not interchangeable descriptions. The scheduler chooses runnable execution entities, while the process abstraction supplies much of their shared environment.

topics.title: 21.2 Process state
topics.summary: A simple state model includes running, runnable, waiting, stopped, and terminated states. Runnable means eligible for CPU execution; running means currently executing. A process waiting for input is not made faster merely by adding more CPU time if the required input has not arrived. A terminated child may temporarily remain as a zombie until its parent collects the termination information. The zombie is not executing the old program. Its remaining bookkeeping supports the parent’s ability to retrieve status. Real kernels expose more detailed states than this teaching model, but the model is sufficient to separate eligibility, execution, and event waiting.

topics.title: 21.3 CPU context
topics.summary: CPU context includes the register and control state needed to resume an execution stream. It encompasses more than the source-level local variables a programmer can name. The instruction pointer, stack pointer, flags, and other architecture-defined state influence what happens next. Not all context is necessarily saved and restored through one identical path. Kernel implementations optimize context handling, and architecture extensions enlarge the state that may need management. For reasoning, the essential requirement is preservation of the execution semantics promised to the program. A resumed thread must not receive another thread’s live register values as though they were its own.

topics.title: 21.4 Address space
topics.summary: An address space defines the virtual mappings visible to a process. It contains executable code, data, stacks, dynamically allocated regions, shared mappings, and reserved or inaccessible gaps. Two processes can map different physical storage at the same virtual address. Conversely, two processes can map the same physical storage at different virtual addresses. This is how shared mappings can coexist with otherwise distinct address spaces. A pointer stored in shared memory is therefore not automatically meaningful in another process. Use offsets or another explicitly designed representation when the same region may appear at different base addresses.

topics.title: 21.5 Process isolation
topics.summary: Isolation limits the ability of one process to read or modify another process’s private state. Page tables and permissions provide a major hardware-backed mechanism. Kernel policy controls explicit exceptions, such as shared mappings and authorized debugging interfaces. Isolation is a security and reliability boundary, but it is not an absolute statement that processes can never communicate or interfere indirectly. They may share files, services, CPU capacity, and other resources. An application must distinguish intentional communication from accidental sharing and must still validate input received across process boundaries.

topics.title: 21.6 Context switching
topics.summary: A context switch changes which execution stream uses a processor. It requires saving and restoring relevant state and may involve changing the active address-space context. Switching between threads in the same process can avoid some address-space changes, but it still has scheduling and execution-state costs. The effects extend beyond the instructions that perform the switch. A different working set can displace useful cache entries or translations. Conversely, a context switch does not imply that all caches are universally flushed. Actual hardware and kernel mechanisms determine which state remains useful. Avoid reducing context-switch cost to one supposedly universal number.

topics.title: 21.7 Scheduling
topics.summary: Scheduling selects runnable work according to policy and constraints. General-purpose scheduling balances responsiveness, fairness, and throughput; real-time policies make different tradeoffs and require careful system-level design. Application priorities do not create CPU capacity that does not exist. A scheduling trace must include waiting as well as computation. A server may consume little CPU because it is blocked on clients, not because it is efficient. A compute-heavy application may scale until it encounters memory bandwidth or synchronization limits. Measure runnable demand, actual execution, and blocking causes separately before changing priorities or thread counts. [ R38 ]

topics.title: Worked example — A scheduling model with waiting
topics.summary: Assume one CPU, zero switching overhead, and a scheduler that gives a newly runnable job the next available opportunity. Job A needs 2 milliseconds of CPU, then waits 5 milliseconds for I/O, then needs 1 millisecond of CPU. Job B needs 4 milliseconds of CPU and never blocks. Both are ready at time zero, and A starts first. A consumes 3 milliseconds of CPU but finishes after 8 milliseconds of wall time. B consumes 4 milliseconds and finishes at time 6. The CPU performs 7 milliseconds of useful work during an 8-millisecond observation interval, giving modeled utilization of 7 / 8 = 87.5% . This calculation assumes that the I/O wait completes at time 7 independently of B. It excludes kernel work, interrupt overhead, and real scheduling details. The point is not to predict a production trace but to establish the vocabulary and accounting needed to interpret one.

workshop.title: Waiting is different from being runnable
workshop.problem: Model process A issuing I/O while process B is ready. A must leave the run queue until its I/O completes.

steps.why: A cannot make progress until an external completion occurs.
A different runnable process can use the CPU while A waits.
Ready means eligible to run, not necessarily running at that instant.

workshop.pitfall: Treating waiting and ready as the same state can make a scheduler repeatedly choose work that cannot progress.

discussion.question: Does B running while A waits require two CPU cores?
discussion.answer: No. One core can switch from A to B. Parallel execution requires simultaneous execution resources; concurrency only requires overlapping work in progress.

workshop.alternative: Sequential execution is simpler when tasks never wait and there is no need to overlap their lifetimes.
workshop.design: A state machine makes the permitted change explicit at each call. Checking the source state prevents an event from pretending a blocked process can run. This generic transition helper trusts its caller to supply the allowed edge; a production scheduler would expose named operations or validate the edge set centrally.
invariants: Waiting does not mean runnable. Completion of the waited-for event makes the process ready; dispatch is a separate step.
workshop.maintenance: Wakeup makes work eligible by moving it to Ready. Dispatch is a separate scheduling decision.

SLIDE 1: Chapter 21 — Processes

LECTURE NARRATION
A process is an operating-system-managed execution environment. It combines an address space, references to resources, credentials, and one or more threads of execution. The abstraction gives a program the appearance of its own machine while allowing the kernel to share actual processors, memory, and devices among many programs. Processes are not identical to executable files. Several processes can run the same executable, and one process can replace its program image with another through exec . A process also need not have exactly one thread. These distinctions become important when considering scheduling, resource ownership, and process creation. [ R15 , R16 , R38 ]

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
In simpler terms, a process is an operating-system-managed execution environment.

Its virtual address space determines which addresses have meaning; its descriptor table determines what small descriptor numbers refer to; its credentials help determine which requests are allowed. Therefore, “switching processes” and “switching threads” are related but not interchangeable descriptions. The scheduler chooses runnable execution entities, while the process abstraction supplies much of their shared environment.

SLIDE 14: 21.6 Context switching

LECTURE NARRATION
A context switch changes which execution stream uses a processor. It requires saving and restoring relevant state and may involve changing the active address-space context. Switching between threads in the same process can avoid some address-space changes, but it still has scheduling and execution-state costs. The effects extend beyond the instructions that perform the switch. A different working set can displace useful cache entries or translations. Conversely, a context switch does not imply that all caches are universally flushed. Actual hardware and kernel mechanisms determine which state remains useful. Avoid reducing context-switch cost to one supposedly universal number.

SLIDE 18: Worked example — A scheduling model with waiting

LECTURE NARRATION
Assume one CPU, zero switching overhead, and a scheduler that gives a newly runnable job the next available opportunity. Job A needs 2 milliseconds of CPU, then waits 5 milliseconds for I/O, then needs 1 millisecond of CPU. Job B needs 4 milliseconds of CPU and never blocks. Both are ready at time zero, and A starts first. A consumes 3 milliseconds of CPU but finishes after 8 milliseconds of wall time. B consumes 4 milliseconds and finishes at time 6. The CPU performs 7 milliseconds of useful work during an 8-millisecond observation interval, giving modeled utilization of 7 / 8 = 87.5% . This calculation assumes that the I/O wait completes at time 7 independently of B. It excludes kernel work, interrupt overhead, and real scheduling details. The point is not to predict a production trace but to establish the vocabulary and accounting needed to interpret one.
